page: Vultr vx1-g-2c-8g is an x86_64 general-purpose server belonging to the VX1 Cloud Compute family. It features 2 vCPUs derived from a single physical AMD EPYC core with 2 threads per core, operating at a clock speed of 2.0 GHz. The CPU allocation is dedicated, supported by 32 MB of L3 cache, 1.0 MB of L2 cache, and 48 KB of L1d cache. The system is equipped with 8.0 GB of RAM, providing a balanced 4.0 GB of memory per core. It utilizes 1 GB of network-attached local storage and includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. No GPU hardware is present.

Benchmark data reveals a stark contrast between single-core and multi-core capabilities. The server achieves top-tier performance in single-core metrics, with stress-ng single-core CPU performance scoring 3688.67 and single-threaded gzip compression reaching 39.96 GB/sec. However, multi-core and memory-intensive benchmarks are significantly weaker. The stress-ng multi-core CPU performance and Geekbench multi-core score both fall into the bottom 25% tier. Memory bandwidth read-only tests also rank in the bottom 25%, though large block write bandwidth remains average at 28.99 GB/sec.

Due to the single physical core architecture, the server struggles with highly parallelized workloads. Passmark database operations rank in the bottom 10%, and Redis SET operations are weak at 3.96 million operations per second. LLM inference is highly constrained, with medium 7B model text generation performing poorly at 6.31 tokens per second. However, static web serving throughput is average at 8.04 GB/sec. This hardware profile is best suited for lightweight, single-threaded applications, basic static web serving, and low-intensity general-purpose tasks rather than database hosting or parallel computing.
description: Vultr vx1-g-2c-8g is an x86_64 general-purpose server from the VX1 Cloud Compute family, configured with 2 dedicated vCPUs from a single physical AMD EPYC core and 8.0 GB of RAM. It relies on 1 GB of network-attached storage and lacks GPU acceleration. Performance benchmarks show a strong divergence: single-core CPU performance and single-threaded compression tasks rank in the top 10%, whereas multi-core execution, memory bandwidth, and database operations fall into the bottom 25% or lower. Consequently, the server is highly efficient for single-threaded applications and static web serving, but exhibits clear performance bottlenecks under multi-threaded, memory-intensive, or database-heavy workloads.
